FAST

DUBLIN, Oct 14 : Recent hacking incidents perpetrated by AI agents are "early warning shots", and the world could soon face major incidents if systems are not made more secure, Google DeepMind co-founder and Chair Demis Hassabis said on Wednesday. Rogue behaviour by AI agents, including corporate network hacks and, most recently, Anthropic's disclosure that an AI model submitted a false homicide tip to police, has prompted warnings from researchers and fueled concerns over the fast-advancing technology. Hassabis said there was "a lot of work to do" to adopt the kind of best practices that other fields such as biology or the nuclear sector use to secure critical systems and that some sort of international standards body would eventually be needed. "I think these (hacking incidents) are early warning shots for us that systems aren't that powerful yet, so the incidents aren't that major," Hassabis, who is also chief scientist at Google parent Alphabet, told an AI summit in Dublin.

"But they could be (major) looking into next year and the next couple years if we don't do more work as an industry, as individual companies and governments on securing these systems." He said that, while an international standards body seemed like an obvious intervention, it would need to be nuanced and nimble so as not to stifle innovation. "So what you need to do is basically build up dynamically this kind of certification process that is proportionate with the risks as we see it and can quickly change depending on where the technology goes," he said.

NEW YORK, Oct 14 : AI skills are starting to count toward pay and promotion on Wall Street, with nearly a quarter of financial firms tying raises, bonuses or promotions to employees’ proficiency with the technology, a survey showed. Another 30 per cent require employees to disclose their use of artificial intelligence tools in formal performance reviews, according to the survey by Selby Jennings, a financial-services recruitment firm. The findings point to a broader shift on Wall Street as firms seek tangible returns from their investment in the technology. "Companies are no longer just seeing if their employees are using AI tools but are also monitoring its impact on output and contribution to business results," Dylan Gomez, executive director at Selby Jennings, told Reuters.

LONDON, Oct 14 : Britain's media regulator Ofcom said on Wednesday it remained concerned about Elon Musk-owned X's handling of illegal hate and terror content and was assessing whether the platform breached online safety laws, despite improvements in response times. X's first quarterly report to Ofcom showed it had met commitments to review suspected illegal hate and terror content within agreed timeframes, with response times improving compared with evidence examined earlier this year. However, the regulator said it had "ongoing concerns" about the effectiveness of X's efforts to remove illegal hate and terror content and had received mixed reports over the company's engagement with third-party experts. The regulator also said that SpaceXAI, formerly xAI, had introduced further restrictions to its standalone Grok AI chatbot service, including measures preventing UK-based users from viewing, generating or sharing pornographic content and barring companion chatbots such as "Ani" from engaging in sexually explicit conversations.

FAST

Oct 14 : Few animals show the link between size and lifespan as clearly as dogs. Within this one species, large breeds such as Great Danes typically die younger than small ones such as Chihuahuas. A new study indicates the reason may lie in how DNA changes with age in dogs. Across mammals, bigger species like elephants usually live longer lives than smaller ones like mice, but within a species that pattern can reverse. Earlier comparisons across species linked certain biological mechanisms to exceptional longevity, but those are less suited to explaining differences among individuals within a species.  "We all know that big dogs usually don't live as long as small dogs, but we have not known whether their cells actually age faster, or whether they simply hit certain diseases earlier," said Noah Snyder-Mackler, a professor at Arizona State University's School of Life Sciences and Center for Evolution and Medicine and one of the authors of the study published in the journal Science.  To find out, the researchers measured DNA methylation, chemical tags that help control which genes are switched on and off. Using age-related patterns in these tags, they built an epigenetic clock that estimated a dog's age with a median error of less than one year.

Analyzing 1,640 blood methylation profiles from 894 pet canines of various breeds, they found that larger dogs and male dogs showed signs of accelerated molecular aging, while dogs whose biological age appeared older than expected based on the profiles faced a higher risk of early death. "We found that large dogs show a faster-moving DNA methylation aging signature in blood, and that this acceleration is especially strong in parts of the genome that normally help keep 'jumping genes' quiet," Snyder-Mackler said.  Jumping genes, also called transposable elements, can copy themselves and insert into new spots in the genome. LINE1s are a type of jumping gene that is normally kept silent by DNA methylation, but their activation has been linked to genome instability, cancer and other age-related disease.  In large dogs, Snyder-Mackler said, "methylation at those regions appears to erode more quickly with age, as if the genome is losing some of the tape or clamps that keep these mobile elements suppressed."  This suggests that the shorter lives of large dogs reflect a faster molecular aging trajectory.  "If large dogs simply died earlier after following the same molecular trajectory, we would look for late-life triggers of disease or mortality. But if parts of the aging program move faster throughout adulthood, as our data suggest for the blood methylome, then there may be processes we can measure, follow over time, and potentially modify before disease appears," Snyder-Mackler said. DIFFERENCES BY SEX The researchers also found differences between male and female dogs, largely on the X chromosome — the sex chromosome that females carry in two copies and males in one. There, LINE1 elements showed higher methylation in males. Chromosomes are thread-like structures that carry genetic information inside cell nuclei. "In our genome-wide analyses, the sex signal looked distinct from the body-size signal, so I would treat that as a separate biology that needs follow-up rather than the same mechanism in disguise," Snyder-Mackler said. The trade-off between large size and longevity may be a consequence of selective breeding rather than natural evolution. Humans bred dogs to grow quickly and reach large adult sizes for tasks such as guarding, hunting and herding.  "If selection strongly favors rapid growth or large adult size before old age, late-life costs can come along for the ride," Snyder-Mackler added. Previous explanations for why large dogs tend to have shorter lives focused on growth biology. Researchers have also suggested that larger dogs may undergo more cell growth, develop more quickly or face a higher risk of cancer.  "Our study does not replace those ideas; it gives us a molecular layer downstream of body size," Snyder-Mackler said. The findings raise the possibility that slowing molecular aging could help extend healthy lifespan in larger dogs. Snyder-Mackler said, however, that lifespan is not governed by a single biological clock. Large dogs would still face breed-specific risks, meaning that slowing molecular aging would not turn a Great Dane into a Chihuahua, in terms of lifespan, but could make one component of its aging trajectory less compressed.

Source: Reuters

FAST

BRUSSELS, Oct 14 : Adult content platform Stripchat, a subsidiary of Cyprus's Technius, on Thursday lost its legal challenge against EU tech regulators' decision to include it in a list of companies subject to stringent requirements under landmark online content rules after Europe's second-highest court rejected its arguments, a court statement said. Three years ago, the European Commission designated Stripchat and two other adult content companies as very large online platforms under the Digital Services Act which requires such companies to do more to tackle illegal and harmful content on their platforms. DSA breaches can cost companies fines as much as 6 per cent of their global turnover. Stripchat subsequently sued the Commission, which is the EU tech enforcer, at the Luxembourg-based General Court. It disagreed with how the Commission calculated its number of users, a benchmark used to assess whether a company falls under the DSA. A court statement stated that the European Commission had given Stripchat adequate reasons for its decision.

KUALA LUMPUR: A Malaysian court on Wednesday (Oct 14) denied former Prime Minister Najib Razak's request to suspend a 15-year jail term in connection with the 1MDB scandal, despite expectations he might be transferred to house arrest f ollowing a pardon in a separate case . Najib has been in prison since 2022 after being convicted of graft and money laundering linked to the alleged theft of billions of dollars from 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB), a state fund he co-founded while premier in 2009. He has denied wrongdoing. In December, Najib was also convicted of abuse of power and money laundering in a separate case and handed a 15-year prison term and US$2.8 billion in fines, which he asked to be suspended pending his appeal . His lawyers argued he was in declining health and that the fines imposed on him were too large to pay, but Judge Noor Ruwena Md Nordin said there were no special circumstances warranting a stay of that sentence.

"The gravity of the offence is a more important public interest consideration, which this court must have regard to," the judge said in dismissing the request. Najib's lawyer Muhammad Shafee Abdullah said he would file a fresh application for a stay at the Court of Appeal. GLOBE-SPANNING SCHEME US investigators have said that around US$4.5 billion was siphoned from 1MDB in a complex, globe-spanning scheme, with more than US$1 billion ending up in accounts linked to Najib. He has said he was misled about the source of the funds he received. Wednesday's decision is a setback for Najib, who last month received a second royal pardon related to his initial conviction, which will allow him to serve the remainder of that sentence at home. The previous king, in 2024, cut his 12-year term in half. Najib's transfer to house arrest is pending payment of a 50 million ringgit (US$12.25 million) fine. His 15-year jail sentence is due to begin after his house arrest ends in August 2028. His political party, the United Malays National Organisation (UMNO), launched a fundraising drive for supporters to help Najib, who says he cannot pay the fine because his bank accounts are frozen . The latest royal pardon has deepened divisions within the administration of Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, which includes the UMNO. Anthony Loke, the leader of the Democratic Action Party, the largest party in Anwar's ruling coalition, offered to resign as transport minister a day after the decision to pardon Najib was announced. Loke has said he would stay in cabinet until Najib starts his house arrest.

FAST

DURBAN, Oct 14 : Age appears no closer to catching up with Australia's veteran bowling attack after the quartet produced yet another decisive performance in the first test against South Africa to put the tourists 1-0 up in the three-match series. While batter Matt Renshaw took the plaudits after scores of 190 and 82 helped Australia to a 214-run win at Kingsmead in Durban on Tuesday, their bowlers skittled South Africa twice to secure the emphatic victory. Josh Hazlewood, 35, returned his best test figures of 6-49 to wrap up the win and received strong support from Pat Cummins, 33, fellow seamer Mitchell Starc, 36, and 38-year-old spinner Nathan Lyon. It is no accident that the four have enjoyed such longevity in the test arena, with captain Cummins praising the bowlers' preparations.

“So much since (last year’s) Ashes has been how are we going to get ourselves to this position and in as good a spot as we can be," Cummins said.  "Before that Darwin test (against Bangladesh in August) we did a lot of work, a big training block to get ahead of the eight ball and pay dividends down the track, which is, I guess, now." There is also buy-in from the bowlers to rest when necessary and Cummins said back-up quicks Scott Boland and Michael Neser, who have been working in the nets, were looking as sharp as the others. After overcoming a hamstring injury, Lyon said he was in the best shape of his career, despite being on the cusp of 39. "The amount of work that I've put in, I've never had any doubt that I'll get back,” he said of a vigorous training programme. "I haven't had any alcohol for a fair while now, but I'm just trying to squeeze as much out of the lemon as possible that I can. "I still feel like there's a lot of decent cricket ahead of me, that's for sure." A CAPTAIN'S DREAM Hazlewood is also back on form after injuries kept him out of the last Ashes. “It couldn’t have gone any better,” he said of his bowling on the last two days in Durban. “I’m a bit older than I used to be, but everything’s feeling good.” Hazlewood now has 311 test wickets and has moved above Brett Lee into eighth in Australia’s all-time list. "He obviously gets spoken about a lot for his consistency, but I think that undersells him," said Cummins. "He's really skilful with the new ball, but once you get a reversing ball, he's just as skilful; he can swing it both ways." The captain also praised Hazlewood and Starc for their willingness to put the team first. “They're just, whatever the team needs, they'll just roll up their sleeves and go to work," he added. "A captain's dream."

(Editing by Peter Rutherford)
